description: Halloween is the deadliest night of the year for children on foot. What Georgia law says about who is responsible, and what to do if your child is hit.
shortAnswer: Halloween is the deadliest night of the year for children on foot. For children ages 4 to 8, the risk was about ten times higher. Georgia law requires every driver to exercise due care to avoid colliding with any pedestrian and to “exercise proper precaution upon observing any child.”

sections.heading: Why Halloween is so dangerous
sections.shortAnswer: It is dark, costumes are dark, and masks block vision. Children dart, many Georgia subdivisions have no sidewalks, and drivers are distracted, rushed, or impaired.

sections.heading: What Georgia law expects of a driver
sections.shortAnswer: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-93 says every driver shall exercise due care to avoid colliding with any pedestrian and shall “exercise proper precaution upon observing any child.” A child who runs into the street mid-block may have broken a pedestrian rule. That does not end the case.

sections.heading: Can my child be blamed?
sections.shortAnswer: It depends on your child’s age. Very young children, four and under, cannot be charged with negligence at all. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-5, a child under 14 is judged by the care that child’s own mental and physical capacity fits him to exercise.

sections.heading: When the driver was drinking
sections.shortAnswer: The punitive damages cap does not apply when the defendant acted while under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-40, the person who served the driver may also be responsible.

sections.heading: When the driver does not stop
sections.shortAnswer: If the driver is never found, your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage may pay. Report the crash to police right away.

sections.heading: Injuries on someone’s porch or yard
sections.shortAnswer: A child who walks up to a neighbor’s door to trick-or-treat is usually treated as a licensee under Georgia law. A business that invites the public in owes ordinary care to keep its premises safe.

sections.heading: If your child is hit: what to do now
sections.shortAnswer: Get your child medical care, get the police report number and witnesses’ names, and ask neighbors for doorbell and security camera video now. Keep the costume. Do not give a recorded statement to the driver’s insurance company before you talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: A few things that actually help
sections.shortAnswer: Give every child a flashlight or a glow stick, use face paint instead of masks, cross at corners, and walk with children under 12. If you are driving, drive like every shadow is a child.

faq.q: How much more dangerous is Halloween for child pedestrians?
faq.a: Researchers writing in JAMA Pediatrics looked at 42 years of fatal crash data. The risk of a pedestrian death was 43 percent higher on Halloween. For children ages 4 to 8, the risk was about ten times higher.

faq.q: Can my child be blamed for running into the street in Georgia?
faq.a: It depends on your child’s age. Very young children, four and under, cannot be charged with negligence at all. For children older than six, it is less clear. Whether a particular child was capable of protecting himself is usually a question for the jury.

faq.q: Can a Halloween party host be liable if a drunk guest hits my child in Georgia?
faq.a: Under Georgia’s dram shop statute, O.C.G.A. § 51-1-40, a person who knowingly serves someone who is noticeably intoxicated, knowing that person will soon be driving, can be liable for the harm that follows. That can include a bar. It can also include the host of a Halloween party.

faq.q: What evidence should I get if my child is hit by a car while trick-or-treating?
faq.a: Ask neighbors for doorbell and security camera video, and ask now. Many systems overwrite footage within days. Get witnesses’ names and phone numbers. Keep the costume. Do not wash it or throw it away.
